summary: Environment family: person entries for William Cronon, Donald Worster, Alfred W. Crosby, Carolyn Merchant and Richard White (the 1990 JAH round table minus Pyne) and precursor entries for Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson; Innis linked to environmental history as a disputed Canadian antecedent (Cook's continuity claim, Forkey's rejection); edge_111 revised from an undirected comparison to an Annales influence acknowledged by Worster and Cronon, reassessed later by McNeill; environment roster rows for Hays, Nash, Pyne, Le Roy Ladurie, Innis and Richard White; edge_720 and edge_336 no longer carry person names.
authorization: User, 2026-10-13: improving the landing-page families is 'the top priority'; Environmental History's two timeline thinkers do 'not represent the field at all'; 'we need careful evaluation of who gets put front and centre in a timeline'; on the evidence table: 'that is the AHA round table minus Pyne, which makes sense; Aldo Leopold and Rachel Carson are key'.
rationale: Evidence in data/extension-2026/environment-family-2026-10-13/: the field's own histories of itself (canon-evidence-international.md, 14 texts), Canadian environmental historiography (canon-evidence-canada.md, 26 texts), and Canadian History PhD citations (canada-us-canon-test/; a narrow slice, user). Cronon, Worster and Crosby are named in nearly every self-account; Merchant and White form the next tier; Leopold is the strongest non-historian precursor, and Carson a catalyst for environmental concern whose book US environmental historians shared. Thoreau is never named as a precursor. Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993) acknowledge the Annales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity; McNeill (2003) later reassesses their treatment of environmental change. Canadian accounts disagree over Innis's staples history as an antecedent: Cook (1990) claims continuity, Forkey (1998) rejects it.

edge_111.relationship: Annales geography and multiple time scales as a source of ideas and a temporal affinity for environmental history, acknowledged by Worster (1990) and Cronon (1993); McNeill (2003) later reassessed the Annales treatment of environmental change while crediting their general approach as inspirational
edge_111.evidence_note: In-period acknowledgements first. Donald Worster, 'Transformations of the Earth' (JAH 1990), note 5. Witnesses: the Portuguese translation (Ambiente & Sociedade 5:2/6:1, 2002–03, p. 42, n. 5; PDF read in full) and Internet Archive full-text-search snippets of Worster's 1993 reprint in The Wealth of Nature (ch. 4, n. 5; p. 226 inferred from the running heads on either side; page images not seen; whether the reprint revised the note was not checked). The English JAH page was not reached. Because the English wording is known only from joined search snippets, it is given here as paraphrase: after reporting White's view that frontier and western history had been the formative influence on the field, Worster names French historians and geographers associated with Annales, particularly Braudel, Febvre and Le Roy Ladurie, as a further important source of ideas, distinct from the Turnerian tradition. The translation reads: 'Uma outra fonte de idéias importante, realmente retirada da influência de Frederick Jackson Turner, tem sido a dos historiadores e geógrafos franceses, particularmente Fernand Braudel, Lucien Febvre e Emmanuel Le Roy Ladurie, todos associados à revista dos Annales' (p. 42, n. 5). William Cronon, 'The Uses of Environmental History' (1993; OCR of the author-hosted page scan, journal pagination), p. 14: 'Perhaps this is why we feel some kinship with a Braudelian vision of history in which the different time scales of la longue durée, la vie matérielle, and l'histoire événementielle weave together to form the tapestry of the past. Although our general bias is often toward the longue durée, we understand that the interactions of environment, economy, political institutions, social norms, cultural values, and natural processes are endlessly complex' (n. 29 cites The Mediterranean). Both acknowledge a source of ideas and a kinship, not a lineage, and neither disputes it. Later reading, not evidence for the 1990–93 claim: J. R. McNeill (2003; text-layer PDF, p. 14 re-read) reassesses the Annales treatment of environmental change, writing that 'the Annales historians were, many of them, strangely blind to evolving environments'; Braudel 'normally imagined it as an unchanging force', while Le Roy Ladurie 'embraced environmental change'; 'To a very limited extent, then, Annales historians were engaged in environmental history avant la lettre'; yet 'Their general approach however proved inspirational for many who would become environmental historians'. Gurevich's chapter (publisher abstract only) supports the Annales side: geography among the school's concerns; it says nothing about environmental history. Earlier wording (an undirected comparison of affinities) is replaced because Worster and Cronon describe influence running from the Annales to the field, not a comparison between equals.

edge_720.relationship: Environmental perspectives on city–hinterland connections, assessed in period by an urban historian as a contribution to urban history (1991–92)
edge_720.evidence_note: In-period evidence: the 1992 Annals of Iowa forum on Nature’s Metropolis (open PDF, text layer read). The urban historian Timothy Mahoney judges that the book 'makes significant theoretical and substantive contributions to both economic and urban history by placing urban and economic development in an environmental context', and that Cronon 'has, perhaps inadvertently, brought urbanization as a “process” forward from its current relegation as a kind of assumed stage set for monographs on local occurrences in cities' (p. 491). Of the premise that 'to really understand how and why cities developed, one must study how they organized their hinterlands', he writes: 'Cronon’s study of Chicago demonstrates the explanatory power of this fundamental urban historical premise' (p. 492). He also finds that in the book 'urban and economic history seem only to serve the interests of environmental history' (p. 491). Cronon’s response: 'One of my most important agendas in Nature’s Metropolis was to try to convince environmental historians that the city is among the most important historical loci of environmental change'; 'Surely such an argument can only strengthen the claims of urban history as a field, setting the process of urbanization in a broader context that is as important to urban historians as it is to environmental ones' (p. 520). The arrow rests on one book, one urban historian’s in-period assessment and the author’s reply; it does not claim that urban history as a field adopted environmental questions. Context only, not support for the claim: Cronon’s 1993 ASEH address names Joel Tarr’s 'many studies of pollution and waste streams' (p. 3, n. 6) and cites Melosi’s Garbage in the Cities (n. 24). cronon_urban_reception (2022) is a later reading. Cronon’s own contribution is the separate edge from his person entry (revision 1.131).

edge_336.relationship: Histories of the Scientific Revolution and of ideas of nature taken into environmental history
edge_336.map_label: Scientific Revolution and ideas of nature
edge_336.evidence_note: History of science supplies environmental history with accounts of how ideas of nature were made and used, here the mechanical philosophy and the domination of nature. The Berkeley retrospective and the reprinted 1980 excerpt document the case mapped; Merchant's own contribution is the separate pair of edges from her person entry (revision 1.131). Pesic’s 1999 abstract supplies a competing reading of Bacon’s metaphor, and Merchant’s 2006 response is a later reading; they document disagreement and do not settle Bacon’s intentions.
